common_name: Americus Hairy Vetch (Late-Maturing High-Biomass Southern Cover Vetch)

planting.note: Sow in early-to-mid fall across the Deep South and Southeast; Americus flowers later than earlier-maturing hairy vetch releases, extending the vegetative growth window before spring termination.

directions: Americus was released in 1993 by the USDA-NRCS Jimmy Carter Plant Materials Center in Americus, Georgia, as a late-maturing winter legume selected for excellent dry matter production across the Southeast. Broadcast or drill inoculated seed into a prepared fall seedbed, ideally paired with a cereal grain like rye or wheat that the vining growth can scramble over for support. Because it flowers later than earlier-maturing hairy vetch releases, it keeps adding biomass and fixing nitrogen later into spring before needing to be terminated ahead of a following crop. Mow, roll, or incorporate at or shortly after flowering, since vetch left to set seed can volunteer as a weed in subsequent plantings.
sources: USDA Natural Resources Conservation Service Plant Materials Program
Jimmy Carter Plant Materials Center, Americus, Georgia
SARE (Sustainable Agriculture Research and Education) — Cover Crop Chart

common_name: Grasslands Puna Chicory (Original New Zealand Forage and Cover Chicory)

planting.note: Sow into a firm, weed-free seedbed in spring or late summer; cover seed only shallowly since it needs light and even moisture to germinate well.

directions: Approved for commercial release in 1985 by New Zealand's DSIR Grasslands Division, Puna was the original forage chicory cultivar that brought this deep-rooted herb into mainstream pasture and cover crop use, later serving as the parent stock for improved selections such as Puna II. It forms a large, deep taproot that breaks up compacted soil and scavenges nutrients and moisture from well below where most grasses root, while its broad, upright leaves provide high crude protein forage. Compared with its descendants it carries somewhat higher levels of bitter sesquiterpene lactones and less uniform winter activity, but it remains a well-documented, productive choice where seed of newer selections isn't available. Graze or mow regularly to keep the stand leafy and prevent bolting.
sources: Journal of Production Agriculture (Volesky, 1996) — Forage Production and Grazing Management of Chicory
University of Kentucky Cooperative Extension AGR-190 — Chicory: An Alternative Livestock Forage

common_name: Celine Camelina (French-Bred Spring Oilseed Cover Crop)

planting.note: Drill into a firm, shallow seedbed as early as the ground can be worked in spring; Celine tolerates light frost as a seedling and is grown as a short-season spring oilseed.

directions: Celine is a French-bred spring camelina cultivar developed by Limagrain and widely used in European and North American agronomic trials as a short-season oilseed rotation crop. Drill it shallowly into a firm, cold seedbed as early in spring as fields are workable, since it germinates well in near-freezing soil. Its deep taproot and drought tolerance let it perform on marginal or dry ground where other spring oilseeds struggle, and its fast canopy closure helps suppress spring weeds. Swath or straight-combine once most pods have dried to a tan color, treating it as a quick cash cover crop ahead of a summer planting.
sources: University of Minnesota Extension — Camelina Production
Canadian Journal of Plant Science — Camelina Cultivar Nitrogen Response Studies
Washington State University Extension — Camelina Variety Trials

common_name: Calena Camelina (Austrian-Bred Spring Oilseed Cover Crop)

planting.note: Drill into a firm, shallow seedbed as early as the ground can be worked; Calena has shown strong seedling cold tolerance in Pacific Northwest and Canadian field trials.

directions: Calena is an Austrian spring camelina cultivar bred and supplied via Saatbau Linz that has shown stable establishment, yield, and oil content across varied environments in Canadian field trials, including seedling cold exposure well below freezing in Pacific Northwest research plots. Drill it into a firm, cool seedbed as early as the ground can be worked in spring, taking advantage of its rapid, cold-tolerant germination. Its dense canopy closes quickly to suppress weeds on marginal ground, and the crop can be swathed or direct-combined once the bulk of the pods have dried. Choose Calena over less cold-hardy spring camelina lines where reliability across unpredictable spring weather matters most.
sources: Canadian Journal of Plant Science — Camelina Cultivar Nitrogen Response Studies, Maritime Provinces of Canada
Washington State University Extension — Camelina Genotype Adaptation Trials
USDA Agricultural Research Service — Camelina Breeding Program

common_name: Springfield Buckwheat (Large-Seeded High-Yield Cover Crop Buckwheat)

planting.note: Broadcast or drill after all danger of frost has passed into warm, workable soil; Springfield is a large-seeded variety bred by Agriculture and Agri-Food Canada at Morden, Manitoba that has performed strongly in North Dakota regional variety trials.

directions: Springfield is a large-seeded buckwheat variety bred at Agriculture and Agri-Food Canada's Morden, Manitoba research station and documented in USDA NRCS cover crop guidance as one of the highest-yielding selections in North Dakota regional trials. Broadcast seed about half an inch deep into a warm, well-worked seedbed once soil has warmed after the last frost, since it germinates within days and canopies quickly enough to smother emerging weeds. Its larger seed size makes it a good dual-purpose choice where some grain harvest alongside soil-building benefit is wanted, though for pure cover crop use it should be mowed or incorporated at first bloom to capture peak biomass before seed set. Like other buckwheat types it draws abundant pollinators during its brief, heavy bloom window.
sources: USDA Natural Resources Conservation Service — Buckwheat Plant Guide (Fagopyrum esculentum)
North Dakota State University Extension — Buckwheat Variety Trials
SARE — Managing Cover Crops Profitably: Buckwheat

common_name: Specter Winter Pea (Extra-Hardy Tall Forage and Cover Crop Pea)

planting.note: Drill or broadcast inoculated seed in fall; Specter is rated among the most winter-hardy field pea cultivars and benefits from a cereal companion to support its tall, sprawling vines.

directions: Specter is an exceptionally winter-hardy, Pacific Northwest-bred field pea selected to survive harsh winter conditions and resume vigorous growth in spring, producing notably more biomass than many older winter pea types. Its long, climbing vines can reach six feet or more, making it a strong dual-purpose forage and cover crop pea; mix it with a cereal grain such as rye or triticale to give the sprawling growth something to climb for better stand structure and easier mechanical termination. Drill inoculated seed into a prepared fall seedbed, since good rhizobia contact is essential for nitrogen fixation. Mow, roll, or graze in spring near flowering to capture peak biomass and nitrogen contribution before pod set.
sources: Forbes Seed — Cover Crop Seed Catalog
Midwest Cover Crops Council — Field Pea Cover Crop Guide
SARE (Sustainable Agriculture Research and Education) — Cover Crop Chart
